```{r include=FALSE}
# the code in this chunk enables us to truncate the print output for each
# chunk using the `out.lines` option
# save the built-in output hook
hook_output <- knitr::knit_hooks$get("output")

# set a new output hook to truncate text output
knitr::knit_hooks$set(output = function(x, options) {
  if (!is.null(n <- options$out.lines)) {
    x <- xfun::split_lines(x)
    if (length(x) > n) {
        
      # truncate the output
      x <- c(head(x, n), "....\n")
    }
    x <- paste(x, collapse = "\n")
  }
  hook_output(x, options)
})
```


# Introduction

*DrugScreenExplorer* is an R package designed for streamlined processing, 
quality control and visualizing of high-throughput drug sensitivity screen data. 

The package can achieve the following functions: 

1, data preprocessing;
2, check and report the quality of the screen data;     
1, normalize the viability values;  
2, detect and adjust the edge effects    
3, summarize drug effects using several measures, e.g., IC50 and AUC  
4, summarize the synergy or antagonism effects of two-drug combination     
6, using a shiny app to explore process data interactively   

*DrugScreenExplorer* was original designed to proceed the single drug screening, 
but now extended to two-drug combinations.    

```{r, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE}
library(DrugScreenExplorer)
library(tidyr)
library(dplyr)
library(gridExtra)
library(ggplot2)
library(tools)
```


# Installation

The *DrugScreenExplorer* package can be installed from  Bioconductor using the 
following commands:

```{r, eval = FALSE}

if (!requireNamespace("BiocManager", quietly = TRUE))
     install.packages("BiocManager")
BiocManager::install("DrugScreenExplorer")

```


# Data import

## Introduction of input file types

For creating the complete drug screen datasets, three types of data are needed:

1) the raw screening data in text format, which stores the values out from a 
plate reader;

2) the well annotation or plate layout, which stores the metadata for all the 
wells on a screening plate. The most important annotations are drug names and 
concentrations;

3) the plate annotation, which stores the metadata for each plate. 
For example, the sample information, if each plate represents one sample.

The examples for each type of the input files can be found in the test data 
affiliated with this package:

**Raw screening data**

```{r}
system.file("testData/rawData", package = "DrugScreenExplorer")
```
If the text files containing the raw screening data are organized by subfolders, 
the subfolders will be considered as batches.

**Plate annotation file**

```{r}
system.file("testData/plateAnno/plateAnno.tsv", package = "DrugScreenExplorer")
```

The *fileName* column is mandatory. If the plates do not all have the same 
layout, for example, several plates are used for the same sample but with 
different drug collections, a *plateID* column can be included to indicate 
the plate index.

**Well annotation file**

```{r}
system.file("testData/wellAnno/wellAnno.tsv", package = "DrugScreenExplorer")
```

The *wellID* column is mandatory. If plates have different layouts, a *plateID* 
column can be used as in the plate annotation file. 

## Functions for creating annotation files

Besides create the well and plate annotations files manually, there are two 
functions can be used to help create the annotation input files.

### createPlateInput()

The function creates a framework for the plate annotation input based on the 
raw data files and folder structure in the raw data folder.

```{r}
rawFolder <- system.file("testData/rawData", package = "DrugScreenExplorer")
```

```{r}
createPlateInput(rawDir = rawFolder,
                 file = "plateAnno.csv",
                 entries = c("sampleID", "patientID"))
plateAnno <- read.csv("./plateAnno.csv", sep = "\t")
head(plateAnno)
```

An csv file named "plateAnno.csv" will be created and it has three columns: 
*fileName*, *sampleID*, and *patientID*. The *fileName* column is automatically 
filled based on the files in the raw data folder, while *sampleID* and 
*patientID* columns need to be filled manually in the created "plateAnno.csv". 

When raw data is saved within sub-folders, each sub-folder representing data 
from distinct batches, the *createPlateInput()* function can search for the 
raw data within each sub-folder and automatically generate batch information 
when *batchAsFolder* is set to *TRUE*. 

```{r, eval=FALSE}
rawFolder <- system.file("testData/rawData", package = "DrugScreenExplorer")
createPlateInput(rawDir = rawFolder,
                 file = "plateAnno.csv",
                 entries = c("sampleID", "patientID"),
                 batchAsFolder = TRUE)

plateAnno <- read.csv("./plateAnno.csv", sep = "\t")
head(plateAnno)

```

In the output *plateAnno.csv* file, there's an additional column *batch*, 
which contains the batch information. Notice that the folder names are not 
used as batch names. Instead, the series of integer numbers will be assigned 
to batches based on the ordering of the folder names. 

### createWellInput()

The function creates the framework for the well annotation input.

```{r, eval=FALSE}
createWellInput(file = "wellAnno.csv", colNum = 24, rowNum = 16,
                entries = c("drug", "concentration"))

wellAnno <- read.csv("wellAnno.csv", sep = "\t")
head(wellAnno)

```

A *wellAnno.csv* file will be created for a 384-well (16\*24) plate. The 
*wellID* is automatically filled by the *drug* and *concentration* columns 
need to be filled manual.

If more than one plate layouts for a sample are used in the screen, for example, 
when one plate is not enough for testing all the drugs, the *platePerSample* 
parameter can be used to specify how many different plate layouts are used for 
each sample.

```{r, eval=FALSE}
createWellInput(file = "wellAnno.csv", colNum = 24, rowNum = 16,
                entries = c("name", "concentration"),
                platePerSample = 2)
```
In the *wellAnno.csv* file, an additional column *plateID* will be created, 
indicating the index of the plate layout type. It is important that a *plateID* 
column must also be created manually in the plate annotation file, to specify 
which plate layout a certain plate is using. 

## Read in the whole experiment

After preparing the raw data folder, the plate annotation file and the well 
annotation file, the whole experiment can be read in using the `readScreen()` 
function.

```{r, message=FALSE}

plateFile <- system.file("testData/plateAnno/plateAnno.tsv",
                         package = "DrugScreenExplorer")

wellFile  <- system.file("testData/wellAnno/wellAnno.tsv",
                         package = "DrugScreenExplorer")

screenData <- readScreen(rawDir = rawFolder, 
                         plateAnnotationFile = plateFile,
                         wellAnnotationFile = wellFile, 
                         rowRange = c(3,18), colRange = 2, 
                         sep = "[;\t]",
                         negWell <- c("DMSO","PBS"), posWell = c())
head(screenData)

```

A tidy table containing the drug screening result and metadata will be created.   

The raw data format may vary across different platforms. *readScreen()* provides 
two arguments *rowRange* and *colRange* specifying the staring and ending 
positions of the numeric data that represent signals. For instance, 
*rowRange = c(3, 18)* and *colRange = 2* indicate that the data spans rows 3 
to 18 and columns 2 to the last column, containing the signal information. 
Argument *sep* can specify delimiters (e.g, "," or "[;\t]"), where regular 
expression is supported. 

The positive control and negative control wells can be defined in *negWell* 
and *posWell*. The input for *negWell* or *posWell* can be either a character 
vector of *wellIDs* or drug names if the *drug* column is given in the well 
annotation file. Wells that are not labeled as positive controls ("pos") or 
negative controls ("neg") will be labelled as "sample" in the "wellType" column 
of the final output table. This column is important for plate-wise normalization.   

The inhibition rate for each well can also be calculated at this stage by 
specifying "normalization = TRUE". Currently, two methods are supported: 
"negatives" and "NPI". The "negative" method calculates the inhibition rate 
by dividing each measurement by the median of negative controls on the same 
plate $x_{normalized} = \frac{x}{Median(x_{neg})}$, where $Median(x_{neg})$ 
represents the median of negative controls; The "NPI" method, which stands 
for "normalized percent inhibition", measures the distance to the positive 
controls against the distance between the negative control and positive 
controls, calculated as 
$x_{normalized} = \frac{x - Median(x_{pos})}{Median(x_{neg}) - Median(x_{pos})}$.


```{r,message=FALSE}
screenData <- readScreen(rawDir = rawFolder, 
                         plateAnnotationFile = plateFile,
                         wellAnnotationFile = wellFile, 
                         rowRange = c(3, 18), colRange = 2, 
                         sep = "[;\t]",
                         negWell <- c("DMSO","PBS"), posWell = c(),
                         normalization = TRUE, method = "negatives", 
                         discardLayer = 2)
head(screenData %>% 
       dplyr::select(wellID, value, sampleID, drug, concentration, wellType, normVal))
```

With "normalization = TRUE", a new column "normVal" is created containing the 
normalized values. Of note, *readScreen()* allows discarding the exterior layer 
wells in order to mitigate the impacts of incubation effect on the negative 
controls. For instance, by specifying *discardLayer = 2*, the two outermost layer 
wells are excluded from control well calculations. *discardLayer = 0* indicates 
that no control wells are excluded.

Inhibition rate can also be calculated later by using *normalizePlate()* 
function. In other words, reading in the screen data and normalization can 
be two separated steps. 

1. Read in the screen data without normalization ("normalization = FALSE").

```{r}
#disable normalization by setting "normalization = FALSE"
screenData <- readScreen(rawDir = rawFolder, plateAnnotationFile = plateFile,
                         wellAnnotationFile = wellFile, 
                         rowRange = c(3,18), 
                         colRange = 2, 
                         sep = "[;\t]",
                         negWell <- c("DMSO","PBS"), posWell = c(),
                         normalization = FALSE)
```

2. Perform normalization

```{r}
screenData <- normalizePlate(screenData, method = "negatives", discardLayer = 2)
head(screenData %>% dplyr::select(wellID, value, sampleID, drug, 
                                  concentration, wellType, normVal))

```

The results one step procedure using *readScreen()* would be identical to the 
output of the two-step procedure by employing *readScreen* and 
*normalizePlate()*.

# Quality control

## Raw count distribution

The *DrugScreenExplorer* package provides several functions for quality control. 
We can use the *plotRawCount()* function to plot the distribution of the raw 
count (signal) of each plate, to check whether a certain plate has a strange 
behavior. 

```{r, fig.height =5, fig.width=6}
g <- plotRawCount(screenData, ifLog10 = TRUE)
plot(g)
```
The plot identifies the plate "CTGLuminescence_P0010_16PB0066" having a lower 
overall counts. 

## Raw count distribution for each well type

If "wellType" column is available, *plotTypeDist()* function can visualize the 
raw count distribution by well types. The resulting plots can provided a rough 
check on whether the distribution is reasonable. For instance, negative controls 
usually have a higher raw counts than the sample wells. 

```{r, fig.height=8, fig.width=10}
g <- plotTypeDist(screenData, ifLog10 = TRUE)
grid.arrange(grobs = g, ncol = 4)
```

## Plate heatmap plot

A more straight forward way to check the screen quality is to plot the signal 
intensity heatmap for each screen. This can be easily achieved by employing 
the *platePlot()*. Heatmaps make it easy to identify screen artifacts, such as 
incubation effects. 

```{r, fig.width = 6, fig.height = 4}

g <- plotPlate(screenData = screenData, plotPlate = "all", plotType = "viability")
grid.arrange(grobs = g[1:4], ncol = 2)

```

*platePlot()* provides heatmap for three types information, namely, 'layout', 
'zscore' and 'viability'. For *plotType = "viability"*, the normalized 
inhibition will be used for the heatmap, i.e the *normVal* column must be in 
the *screenData* object. Alternatively, *platePlot()* visualizes the Z-scores 
($Z_i = (x_i - \hat{x})/ sd(x)$), if *plotType = "zscore"* . 

<!-- For unnormalized values, per-plate z-score can be used for heatmap plot. -->

```{r, fig.width = 10, fig.height = 8}
g <- plotPlate(screenData = screenData, plotPlate = "all", plotType = "zscore")
grid.arrange(grobs = g, ncol = 4)
```

The *platePlot* function can also be used to plot the plate layout, by 
specifying the *type* parameter as "layout". The resulting plot provides an 
intuitive representation of the well types and their layout on the plate.

```{r, fig.height = 8, fig.width = 10}
g <- plotPlate(screenData = screenData, plotPlate = "all", plotType = "layout")
grid.arrange(grobs = g, ncol = 4)
```

## Automatic screen quality report

An html Rmarkdown report on the screen quality can be automatically generated 
by using the *makeReport* function. Depend on the annotations included in the 
screen data tidy table, different quality check items will be included in the 
report.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
makeReport(screenData = screenData, showCode = FALSE, 
           title = "Report for my drug screening project",
           author = "Junyan Lu", ifPlatePlot = TRUE)
```

An html file will be created in *report* folder under the working directory.   
The information on more customizable options can be found at the manual page 
for *makeReport*

# Adjusting incubation / edge effects

From the plate heatmap plots above, we can observe obvious artifacts. For 
example, some wells in a certain region show significantly higher or lower 
signal intensity. This is known as the incubation effect. Those artifacts 
are typically caused by technical problems, like solvent evaporation, 
pipetting issues, etc.,. If those problematic wells are only located on the 
edge of the plate, it is also called the edge effect.  

Plates show typical incubation effect and edge effect.

```{r, fig.width=10, fig.height=3}

plotPlates <- c("CTGLuminescence_P0021_13PB0035", 
                "CTGLuminescence_P0010_15PB0023")

subScreen <- dplyr::filter(screenData, fileName %in% plotPlates)
g <- plotPlate(subScreen, plotPlate = "all", plotType = "viability")
grid.arrange(grobs = g[c(2, 1)], ncol = 2)

```

The left plate shows the edge effect, where wells located on the edge generally 
exhibit lower values compared to the middle well. The right plate demonstrates 
an incubation effect where the left half displays higher values than the right 
half.

DrugScreenExplorer package provides two functions *fitEdgeEffect* and 
*correctEdgeEffect* for estimating and correcting incubation effect or edge 
effect on the plate. 

*fitEdgeEffect* provides two methods for estimating the edge effects, namely 
**loess** and **sigmoid**. The former utilizes the local regression, while the 
latter uses a 2D-sigmoid model with well locations being the input values. 

Typically, we can firstly employ the **fitEdgeEffect()** function to assess the 
edge effects. After that, **correctEdgeEffect()** can be used to adjusted the 
inhibition values by removing the estimated edge effects. 


```{r}
subScreen <- fitEdgeEffect(subScreen, method = "loess", useNeg = TRUE,
                           useLowConcentrations = 1, span = 1)
```

The estimated incubation effect will be stored in the *edgeFactor* column.  
*useNeg = TRUE* means only negative control wells are used for incubation effect 
estimation. *useLowConcentrations = 1* means the lowest 1 concentration of the 
drugs is also considered as the *de facto* negative controls and used for 
incubation effect estimation. Please refer to the manual page for more 
explanations of the parameters.

The incubation (edge) effect can be visualized using the *platePlot* function 
by specifying *plotType = "edgeEffect"*. 

```{r, fig.width=10, fig.height=3}
g <- plotPlate(subScreen, plotType = "edgeEffect")
grid.arrange(grobs = g[c(2, 1)], ncol =2)
```

The edge effects can be removed from the screen plate using 
*correctEdgeEffect()* function. 

```{r}
subScreen <- correctEdgeEffect(subScreen, correctMethod = "bliss")
```

*correctEdgeEffect()* provides two options for adjusting the edge effects: 
"bliss" and "linear". Bliss simply divides the normalized signal intensity 
by the estimated edge effect intensity. If linear is selected, the correction 
process will be smoothed by a linear function depends on the original 
normalized signal intensity. This option is suitable for the situation when 
the edge effect is very strong and results in instability in the correction 
process. In this example, the edge effect will be removed by Bliss drug 
combination model. The corrected value is stored in a new column *normVal.cor*. 

Currently, the estimation and correction of incubation effect can only be 
performed on normalized values The corrected values can also be visualized 
by *platePlot* function, by specifying *plotType = "viability"* and 
*ifCorrected = TRUE*

```{r, fig.width=10, fig.height=3}
g <- plotPlate(subScreen, plotType = "viability", ifCorrected = TRUE)
grid.arrange(grobs = g, ncol =2)
```

Now the incubation effect has been largely removed.

**Adjust edge effect for the whole screening data**

```{r}
screenData <- correctEdgeEffect(screenData, correctMethod = "bliss")
```

Drug effects can be evaluated using the half-maximal inhibitory concentration 
(IC50). *DrugScreenExplorer* provides the *fitIC50()* function for calculating 
the IC50. *fitIC50* is developed from *dr4pl* package, where inhibitory 
concentration is derived by fitting a parameter logistic model. 

# Summarisation of drug effect

```{r, fig.height = 8, fig.width = 8}
screenData <- summariseScreen(screenData, method = c("average", "AUC"))

sumDat <- screenData %>% 
  select(sampleID, drug, meanViab, AUC) %>% 
  distinct(sampleID, drug, .keep_all = TRUE) %>% 
  pivot_longer(cols = c("meanViab", "AUC"),
               names_to = "method") %>% 
  na.omit()

ggplot(sumDat, aes(x = drug, y = value)) + 
  geom_boxplot(fill = "#7FFFD4") + 
  coord_flip() + 
  theme_bw() + 
  xlab("") + 
  facet_grid( ~ method)
  
```

# Extension to two-drug combination

*DrugScreenExplorer* allows to summarize the synergy or antagonism effects of 
two-drug combination. The combination effects can be estimated by two methods
between *bliss* or *bayesynergy*.  



```{r}

plateFile <- system.file("testData/plateAnnoCombine/plateAnnoCombine.tsv",
                         package = "DrugScreenExplorer")

wellFile  <- system.file("testData/wellAnnoCombine/wellAnnoCombine.tsv",
                         package = "DrugScreenExplorer")

rawFolder <- system.file("testData/rawDataCombine", 
                         package = "DrugScreenExplorer")

screenData <- readScreen(rawDir = rawFolder, 
                         plateAnnotationFile = plateFile,
                         wellAnnotationFile = wellFile, 
                         rowRange = c(7, 22), colRange = 2, 
                         sep = ",",
                         negWell = c("DMSO_DMSO"), posWell = c(),
                         normalization = TRUE)
head(screenData)


```


For *bliss* method, the expected combined effects $V_{AB}$ under bliss 
independence is $ V_{AB}^{bliss} = V_A \times V_B$, where $V_A$ and $V_B$ are the 
viability [@zhao2014new; @grewelle2021statistical]. 


If observed effect $V_{AB}^{obs}$ is lower than $V_{AB}^{bliss}$, the combination 
is synergistic; otherwise additive if $V_{AB}^{obs} = V_{AB}^{bliss}$ or 
antagonistic if $V_{AB}^{obs} > V_{AB}^{bliss}$. 


```{r}

sumScreen <- summariseScreenCombination(screenData,
                                        negDrug = "DMSO",
                                        method = "bliss")

# remove single drug well 
sumScreen %>%
  filter(drug != "DMSO" & drug2 != "DMSO") %>%
  select(drug, concentration, drug2, concentration2, viabObs, viabExp, CI) %>%
  mutate(across(viabObs:CI, ~ round(., 3))) %>%
  head()

```


The **CI** in the table is defined as: $CI = viabObs - viabExp$, where *viabObs* 
and *viabExp* are Observed viability ($V_{AB}^{obs}$) and Expected viability
$V_{AB}^{bliss}$. 

- If \( CI > 0 \): **Antagonism**
- If \( CI = 0 \): **Additive / Independent**
- If \( CI < 0 \): **Synergy**


The *bayesynergy* method models drug combination effects using a Bayesian 
statistical approach. It is designed to distinguish between synergistic, 
antagonistic, and additive interactions between two drugs.*bayesynergy* 
provides a flexible and robust framework; however, it is typically more 
computationally intensive, especially when applied to high-throughput drug 
screening data. 


Of note, the *bayesynergy* package need to be installed manually from 
*https://github.com/ocbe-uio/bayesynergy* if *bayesynergy* methods is selected 
to assess the drug combination effects. 


# Interactive data exploration using Shiny app


An R Shiny application was developed based on the analysis tools in the 
*DrugScreenExplorer* package, enabling users of all technical backgrounds 
to perform comprehensive drug screen analyses through an interactive web 
interface. The application can be launched using the *runShiny()* or 
*makeShiny()* functions. For detailed instructions on using the R Shiny 
application, please refer to the corresponding vignette.
